content: Infection with the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica is prevalent in lowand middle-income countries, and severe cases result in up to 100,000 deaths annually. Effective treatment for amoebic colitis is essential to alleviate symptoms, prevent complications and extraintestinal spread, and reduce transmission rates. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of antiamoebic drugs in treating amoebic colitis. A comprehensive search of the literature was conducted up to March 22, 2018, using databases such as the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and mRCT, as well as conference proceedings. Researchers, organizations, and pharmaceutical companies were contacted, and reference lists were reviewed to identify relevant studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared antiamoebic drugs, either alone or in combination, against placebo or other antiamoebic drugs in adults and children diagnosed with amoebic colitis. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and methodological quality of the trials, extracted data, and analyzed outcomes. Clinical and parasitological failure rates, relapse rates, and adverse events were calculated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using a random-effects model. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed, and subgroup analyses were performed to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of the findings based on trial quality. A total of 41 trials involving 4,999 participants met the inclusion criteria. This update added four new trials to the 37 included in the original review. Notably, 30 of these trials were published over 20 years ago. Only one trial employed adequate methods for randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, and analysis of all randomized participants. Furthermore, only one trial utilized an E. histolytica stool antigen test, and two trials used amoebic culture methods. The evidence suggests that tinidazole may be more effective than metronidazole in reducing clinical failure (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.51; 477 participants, 8 trials; low-certainty evidence). Tinidazole is also likely associated with fewer adverse events compared to metronidazole (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.92; 477 participants, 8 trials; moderate-certainty evidence). Combination therapy, when compared to metronidazole alone, may result in fewer parasitological failures (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.86; 720 participants, 3 trials; low-certainty evidence). However, there is insufficient evidence to determine which specific combination therapy is most effective. Additionally, the evidence is inadequate to draw conclusions about the efficacy of other antiamoebic drugs. In conclusion, tinidazole may be more effective than metronidazole in reducing clinical failure and may cause fewer adverse events. Combination therapy may be more effective in reducing parasitological failure compared to metronidazole alone. However, these findings are primarily based on small trials conducted over two decades ago, many of which had poorly defined outcomes. There is a critical need for more accurate diagnostic tests for E. histolytica, particularly in regions where co-infections with other bacteria and parasites are common.
